summary: A landlocked country in Central Europe, formerly part of the Kingdom of Bohemia and of Austria-Hungary; it separated peacefully from Slovakia in 1993 and is known for its beer and old-town architecture.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The Czech Republic is one of the most secularized countries in the world, for historical reasons: after the Reformation pioneer Jan Hus was burned at the stake in 1415, the Hussites long resisted the papacy; after the Battle of White Mountain in 1620 the Habsburg dynasty forced the whole country to re-Catholicize, so Catholicism came to be seen as a symbol of foreign oppression. After independence in 1918 large numbers left the Church, and from 1948 to 1989 the communist regime again suppressed religion and enforced atheist education, so several generations no longer had any religious transmission.

ranking.name: Undeclared
ranking.description: The religion question in the Czech census is voluntary, and in the 2021 census nearly three-tenths of people chose not to answer. This reflects the widespread Czech view of faith as a private matter and is also related to wariness about religious identity from the communist era; in practice most of them are thought to be close to the non-religious.

ranking.name: Believers not belonging to a specific church
ranking.description: Beginning with the 2011 census, an option of “believer but not belonging to any church” was added, chosen by about one-tenth. Many Czechs are skeptical of organized churches but still believe in some kind of spiritual or supernatural force; this “belief without belonging” is especially common in the Czech lands, which experienced the Hussite movement and an anticlerical tradition.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: In 863 the brothers Cyril and Methodius preached in Great Moravia, in 973 a diocese was established in Prague, and Saint Wenceslas became the nation’s patron. After the Battle of White Mountain Catholicism became the only legal religion, but in the communist era church property was confiscated and clergy were imprisoned, and the proportion of believers fell from about four-tenths in 1991 to under one-tenth today, being more concentrated in rural areas such as South Moravia.

ranking.name: Other Christian
ranking.description: These include the Evangelical Church of Czech Brethren, formed in 1918 by the merger of Lutherans and Reformed and inheriting the traditions of the Hussites and the Bohemian Brethren (to which Comenius belonged); the Czechoslovak Hussite Church, which split from Catholicism in 1920; and also Orthodox and recent immigrant churches, all of them very small.

religion.background: Bohemia accepted Christianity in the 9th–10th centuries, and in the 15th century the Hussite movement made it one of the first regions in Europe to challenge the papacy. After the Battle of White Mountain in 1620, the Habsburgs restored Catholicism by force, and Protestant nobles and intellectuals were driven into exile. This history led many Czechs to link Catholicism with alien rule; after the founding of the state in 1918 an anticlerical tide flourished, and from 1948 the communist regime suppressed religion more systematically. After the Velvet Revolution of 1989 religious freedom was restored, but believers did not return, and non-religion became the mainstream.

ranking.name: Czech
ranking.description: Czech belongs to the West Slavic branch; written documents began to appear in the 13th–14th centuries, in the early 15th century Jan Hus promoted an orthography that marks sounds with diacritics, and the Kralice Bible, published in 1579–1593, established the written standard. Under Habsburg rule German for a time replaced Czech as the language of administration and the upper classes; during the 19th-century “National Revival,” Josef Jungmann compiled a dictionary, which allowed Czech to become once again a language of literature and education. After 1945 about three million ethnic Germans were expelled, and the Czech lands became almost a single-language country.

ranking.name: Slovak
ranking.description: From 1918 to 1992 the Czechs and Slovaks belonged to the same state, Czechoslovakia, the two languages are highly mutually intelligible, and radio and television long ran in both languages in parallel. After the “Velvet Divorce” of 1993, many Slovaks still remained in the Czech Republic to work and study, and Slovak can be used directly in official settings; it is one of the largest minority languages.

ranking.name: Ukrainian
ranking.description: Beginning in the 1990s, large numbers of Ukrainians went to the Czech Republic to work in construction and manufacturing. After Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the Czech Republic took in several hundred thousand Ukrainian refugees, one of the largest numbers in Europe in proportion to population, so Ukrainian has rapidly become more common in the major cities.

language.history: The Slavs migrated into Bohemia and Moravia around the 6th century, and in the 9th century Cyril and Methodius brought a Slavic liturgical script. In the late Middle Ages Czech became a literary language, and Hus reformed the orthography. After the Battle of White Mountain in 1620 Germanization grew worse, and in 1784 Joseph II even made German the language of administration. The National Revival of the 19th century returned Czech to schools and theaters, and in 1918 it became the national language. After World War II the expulsion of the ethnic Germans, together with Slovakia’s separation, made Czech the mother tongue of the overwhelming majority today.

ranking.name: Svíčková (beef sirloin in cream sauce)
ranking.description: Root vegetables such as carrot, celery root and parsnip are stewed together with beef sirloin, then the vegetables are blended into a creamy sauce and poured over slices of meat, served with bread dumplings, cranberry sauce and whipped cream.
ranking.history: The name comes from “svíčková,” which refers to the cut of beef sirloin. The dish arose in the middle-class Czech households of the Austro-Hungarian period in the 19th century, when Czech-language cookbooks published by writers such as Magdalena Dobromila Rettigová gave native home cooking a systematic record. Because it takes time to prepare, it was traditionally served only on Sundays or on important occasions such as weddings, and the sweet-and-sour pairing of cream and cranberry reflects the influence of Viennese court cuisine. Many Czechs still regard it as the most representative festive dish.

ranking.name: Vepřo knedlo zelo (roast pork with dumplings and sauerkraut)
ranking.description: A classic set meal of roast pork, sliced dumplings (knedlíky) and stewed sauerkraut, eaten with roast gravy poured over it.
ranking.history: The name is a colloquial abbreviation of the three words “pork, dumplings, sauerkraut,” and it is often called the Czech national dish. Bohemian farm families commonly kept pigs and entertained guests with roast pork after winter slaughter, while cabbage was pickled into sauerkraut to get through the long winter. The way dumplings are made is closely tied to culinary exchange within Austria-Hungary. In the communist era it was the standard dish in factory and school canteens, and it remains a signature of Sunday family lunches and pubs, often paired with Pilsner beer.

ranking.name: Smažený sýr (fried cheese)
ranking.description: Thick slices of Edam or Czech white-mold cheese are coated in flour, egg and breadcrumbs and deep-fried, crisp outside and molten inside, eaten with fries and tartar sauce.
ranking.history: Fried cheese began to spread in the Czech lands in the mid-20th century; in the communist era the meat supply was unstable, and cheap, filling fried cheese became a popular dish in canteens, pubs and roadside stands. It was originally regarded as a budget substitute for the meat cutlet, and later became vegetarians’ main choice within a traditional meat-eating culture. Today it is seen as the Czech national fast food and is a representative of student gatherings and late-night snacks.

ranking.name: Czech goulash (Guláš)
ranking.description: Beef, onion and paprika are stewed for a long time into a thick sauce, richer than the Hungarian version, and eaten with dumplings or bread.
ranking.history: Goulash originated as the stew of Hungarian steppe herdsmen and spread widely within Austria-Hungary in the 19th century; after reaching the Czech lands it gradually became a thick meat stew rather than a soup. The Czech version often includes beer or large amounts of onion and became one of the most common dishes to accompany drinks in pubs. After Pilsner beer was born in 1842, Czech beer culture and such hearty stews complemented each other, and it remains a must on pub menus.

ranking.name: Koláče
ranking.description: Round cakes of sweet yeast dough, with a filling in the center of poppy seed, plum jam, sweet white cheese or fruit, baked and sprinkled with butter streusel, soft and sweet to eat.
ranking.history: The name comes from the Czech “kolo” (wheel, circle) and can be traced to medieval wedding and festival breads. In Moravia, large numbers of small koláče are handed out to guests and neighbors at weddings, an important social custom. In the 19th century Czech immigrants carried it to Texas in the United States, where it evolved into the popular local “kolache,” and the town of West, Texas, still holds an annual festival about it. In the Czech lands it remains a traditional dessert of weekend family baking and of the holiday table.
